name: Self-destruct
summary: The unit turns itself into the weapon: on a key, or by driving into a target, it blows up, damaging everything around it, and is spent. Because the price is the unit itself, the blast hits far harder than its guns could, and the drama is in the approach, since it has to arrive alive. Common shapes: lock down and charge behind a loud warning (the M.A.D. Tank stops for a long countdown while its crewman runs off), go off on contact (bomb trucks, banelings), or eject and let the empty shell blow a moment later. Many also explode when they are destroyed, so shooting one near your own side backfires, and bombs bunched together set each other off.
counterplay: Kill it at range before it arrives: most carriers are fragile or slow, and many have no other weapon.
Kill it far from your own side: carriers that blow up when destroyed hurt whatever is near them, and careless players have lost their own bases that way.
Get out of the ring or behind cover during the countdown: a locked-down carrier can't follow, and in Overwatch any cover blocks D.Va's blast.
Spread out, and catch bunched carriers together, since one blast can set off the rest.
Make the threatened units immune for the moment, or block the blast with a barrier.
Field units the blast can't hurt: soldiers against the M.A.D. Tank.

other_examples.note: A light, remotely driven truck carrying an atomic bomb. Ordered at a unit, a building or a patch of ground, it drives there and goes off; it also goes off when destroyed, so an air strike on it inside its own base wrecks that base, and trucks parked together set each other off. Air strikes and mines are the recommended answers, and the Iron Curtain can't protect it. It is the ram-on-contact form with a death blast.

sources.title: Demolition truck (Aftermath), Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: Its quote box copies the Demolition Truck paragraph of the Aftermath manual (Westwood, 1997).

other_examples.note: A fairly tough, fast suicide truck that rams into enemies and explodes. It can disguise itself as any vehicle its owner can see, and each truck can be upgraded with a bigger charge or a toxic residue that lingers after the blast. Its high price for a one-shot unit makes target choice matter; an alert player spots it by the way it moves.

A cheap suicide unit morphed from a zergling. It bursts on contact, on command or when killed, splashing nearby enemies (light units especially) but never its own side. It can burrow and wait under an enemy's path. The answers are splitting units apart, siege tanks and widow mines that kill it at range, and tougher armoured units placed in front.

A tiny remote-controlled bomb bought with munitions. Its owner steers it in and sets it off by hand; one can wreck a tank or a tight group of infantry. It also blows up when destroyed, hurting friends nearby, Goliaths bunched together chain-react, it camouflages when parked in heavy cover, and it can't be repaired. The remote-bomb form.

shooter_analogues.note: An ultimate: the pilot ejects and the empty mech explodes a few seconds later over a wide area. Any cover between a target and the mech blocks the blast, and barriers or a field that stops allies dying can cancel it, so teams pair it with stuns, slows or pulls that hold enemies in the open; boosters can launch the mech into position. The pilot fights on foot until a new mech is ready.

player_translation.summary: A slow, lightly armed unit that is one big bomb. Get it into the enemy and press the key: it locks in place behind a loud countdown (or goes off on contact in the ram variant), you bail out as your infantry form, and the blast wrecks what is around it. One blast per life.
as_user: Your whole life is the approach: cover, escorts and timing get you into the enemy's clump; dying on the way wastes the purchase.
Pressing the key commits you: there is no cancel and no moving in the countdown form, so you choose the spot before you press.
You hop out when the countdown starts and run for cover as your infantry form; the kills still count as yours.
Your own team's units in the ring get hurt too (unless the card says otherwise), so you warn them first.
as_target: A siren and a ring on the ground show when and where it will go off: leave the ring, get behind cover, or kill the carrier first.
Killing the carrier before the countdown ends stops the blast in the countdown form; in the death-blast variant it explodes where it dies, so kill it far from your friends.
Spread out when you hear one coming; a tight group loses the most.
teammates: Escorts clear the carrier's counters (enemy soldiers, for the M.A.D. Tank) and soak fire on the way in.
Setups keep enemies in the ring: stuns, slows, pulls and walls that pin them in the open.
Defenders answer with barriers, invulnerability or a 'can't die' field timed to the blast, and healers stand ready for afterwards.
Repairers on the user's side can't save the carrier once it is committed, so the team decides together when to send it.
controls: Q (a short hold to arm, so it can't go off by a misclick): start the self-destruct. One counted key with a per-life cooldown.
Ram variant: drive into an enemy to set it off on contact, or press Q to detonate where you are.
Bailing out happens on its own when the countdown starts; the universal bail-out key (hold X) still works before you arm it.
feedback: A ring on the ground showing the blast's reach, a countdown on the carrier and a rising alarm that everyone on screen hears; the ring is in team colour for allies and red for enemies.
A visible charging animation (a piston pumping faster, a glowing core) so the time left reads from above.
In the death-blast variant a small hazard icon over the carrier at all times, so enemies know not to kill it among their friends.
changes_from_rts: Red Alert's M.A.D. crewman climbs out as an unarmed technician; here the player ejects as their infantry form and keeps the credit for the blast.
The blast's reach must fit on one screen; the M.A.D. pulse reaches past the tank's own sight.
RTS carriers are bought and spent; here the blast is once per life, so the unit's price pays for one try.
The countdown stays unstoppable except by killing the carrier, but is cut to a few seconds: long enough to escape, short enough to stay exciting.
Exploding when killed and chain reactions become variants, not the default, because an enemy killing you to blow up your own team is a big swing.

team_play.notes: The carrier needs escorts to arrive and setups to hold enemies in the ring; defenders need cover, spacing and a timed protection to answer it; the death-blast variant turns killing it into a positioning problem.

notes: A timed area-damage event that also kills the user, with a ring and a countdown, is a small amount of new logic.
Bailing out needs the infantry form to spawn safely next to the carrier at the start of the countdown.
Line-of-sight checks for cover, a friendly-fire flag and an optional chain-reaction rule are the main extras.
Kill credit must go to the player even though their unit died in the blast.
A single blast can trade one unit for several more expensive ones; price, the countdown and per-life use are the brakes.
Cheap ram carriers in numbers (a swarm) can overwhelm defences that are tuned for one at a time.
Friendly fire can be griefed: a carrier that sets off next to its own team.
Disguised or burrowed carriers remove the warning that makes the pattern fair.
The countdown form reads well (a ring and a siren); the ram and disguised forms give far less warning.
Whether a carrier explodes when killed must be visible on it, or players get punished for doing the right thing.

variants.name: Lock down and charge
variants.summary: You stop where you are and a loud countdown runs; only destroying you first stops the blast, and then nothing explodes.

countered_by.why: Long-range guns destroy it during its countdown, which stops the blast altogether.
Fast units leave the ring before the countdown ends.
Units made immune shrug off the blast, and in Red Alert an invulnerable carrier can't even finish its countdown.

variants.name: Ram and blow
variants.summary: Drive into the target and blow up on contact; quick and hard to dodge, but the carrier must reach the target alive.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert Demolition Truck; Generals Bomb Truck; StarCraft II Baneling

variants.name: Eject and blow
variants.summary: The pilot ejects and the empty shell explodes a moment later, so the player fights on foot until they can get a new vehicle.
variants.seen_in: Overwatch 2 D.Va; the M.A.D. Tank's crewman, who leaves as the countdown starts

variants.name: Explodes when killed
variants.summary: The carrier also goes off when destroyed, wherever it is, so the enemy must kill it far from their own units.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert Demolition Truck; Company of Heroes Goliath; StarCraft II Baneling

adds_strengths.why: One blast deals far more damage around it than its guns could, enough to break a group or a defence.
Killing it among its targets still sets off the blast, so the enemy can't safely shoot it up close.

variants.name: Chain reaction
variants.summary: One blast sets off any other carrier inside it, friend or foe, so bombs must keep apart.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert Demolition Truck; Company of Heroes Goliath

adds_weaknesses.why: The blast uses up the unit, so it must reach its target alive and gets one try per life.
Carriers bunched together all go off when one is hit, so they can't move as a group.

variants.name: Disguised bomb
variants.summary: The carrier looks like an ordinary vehicle until it strikes; detection or a sharp eye on how it moves gives it away.

countered_by.why: Detection strips the disguise and shows the bomb for what it is before it gets close.
Once the disguise is seen through, long-range guns kill the carrier on its way in, before it can reach anyone.
Fast units leave the blast area before it goes off.
Units made immune for the moment shrug off the blast, wasting the carrier's one try.

variants.name: Remote bomb
variants.summary: The player steers a small expendable bomb from a safe spot and detonates it by hand, then returns to their own body.
variants.seen_in: Company of Heroes Goliath; Red Alert Demolition Truck (remotely driven)

variants.name: Buried trap
variants.summary: The carrier burrows or hides in cover and waits under the enemy's path, then goes off when they walk over it.
variants.seen_in: StarCraft II Baneling (burrowed); Company of Heroes Goliath (camouflaged in cover)

countered_by.why: Detection reveals the hidden carrier so it can be shot before anyone walks over it.
Once the hidden carrier is found, long-range guns destroy it before anyone walks over it.
Fast units leave the blast area before it goes off.
Units made immune for the moment shrug off the blast, wasting the carrier's one try.

adds_strengths.why: One blast deals far more damage around it than its guns could, enough to break a group or a defence.

adds_weaknesses.why: The blast uses up the unit, so it must reach its target alive and gets one try per life.

counters.why: Slow units can't get out of the blast before it goes off.
Buildings and fixed defences can't dodge it at all.

countered_by.why: Long-range guns kill the carrier on its way in, before it can reach anyone.
Fast units leave the blast area before it goes off.
Units made immune for the moment shrug off the blast, wasting the carrier's one try.

open_questions: Should a carrier explode when killed by default (the RTS norm), or only in the death-blast variant?
After the blast, does the player fight on as their infantry form (bail-out, as the M.A.D. crewman does) or go back to the buy screen?
Friendly fire on by default (Red Alert) or off (StarCraft II Baneling)?
Should infantry be able to roll it at all, given how a soldier blowing himself up reads? It is kept rare here.

shooter_fit.reason: Proven in hero shooters: a loud, readable countdown creates scramble-for-cover moments, escort play on the way in and combo setups that hold enemies in the ring, and one try per life keeps it fair.
